topics.title: Design a database schema for an application with ER diagram from a problem description
topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PCCSL408 - DBMS LAB > - **Module:** Module Experiment 2 > - **Topic:** Design a database schema for an application with ER diagram from a problem description # 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition > [!IMPORTANT] > **Entity-Relationship (ER) Modeling** is a conceptual data modeling technique introduced by **Peter Chen (1976)** that uses a diagrammatic representation to capture the logical structure of a database. It identifies **entities** (real-world objects), **attributes** (properties of entities), and **relationships** (associations between entities) before any physical database implementation begins. A **Database Schema** is the formal blueprint of how data is organized. It defines **tables (relations)**, **columns (attributes)**, **data types**, **constraints** (primary key, foreign key, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK), and the **relationships** among tables using referential integrity. In the **KTU 2024 DBMS Lab syllabus (PCCSL408)**, Experiment 2 specifically tests the student's ability to: 1. Read a natural-language problem statement. 2. Identify entities, attributes, and relationships. 3. Draw an **ER diagram** using **Chen's notation** or **Crow's Foot notation**. 4. Convert the ER diagram into a **relational schema** using standard mapping rules. 5. Optionally implement the schema as **SQL `CREATE TABLE`** statements. ## 1.2 Key Terminology (KTU 2024 Glossary) | Term | Definition | Example | |------|------------|---------| | **Entity** | A real-world object with independent existence | Student, Book, Department | | **Entity Set** | Collection of similar entities | All Students in a University | | **Attribute** | A property describing an entity | Student.name, Book.price | | **Primary Key** | Attribute that uniquely identifies an entity | Student.roll_no | | **Relationship** | An association among entities | Student **enrolls in** Course | | **Cardinality** | Number of entity instances participating | 1:1, 1:N, M:N | | **Participation** | Whether all entities participate (total) or some (partial) | Total vs Partial | | **Weak Entity** | An entity that cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes | Dependent (of Employee) | ## 1.3 Intuitive Real-World Analogy > [!NOTE] > **Analogy: Designing a House Before Construction** > > Imagine you want to build a house. Before laying a single brick, an architect creates a **blueprint** showing rooms (entities), their features like doors and windows (attributes), and how rooms connect (relationships). You would never start construction without this plan. > > An **ER diagram is exactly that blueprint for a database**. The *rooms* are your **tables** (Student, Course, Department). The *features* are your **columns** (name, id, credits). The *connections* are your **foreign keys and JOINs** (a Student *enrolls in* a Course). Just as a missing room in a blueprint means a missing feature in the house, a missing entity in an ER diagram means a missing table in your database. ## 1.4 Two Standard Notations Used in KTU Exams | Notation | Visual Style | Most Common Use | |----------|--------------|-----------------| | **Chen's Notation** | Rectangles (entities), Diamonds (relationships), Ovals (attributes) | Academic textbooks, KTU theory papers | | **Crow's Foot Notation** | Boxes with crow's foot symbols (>, |, <) at line ends | Industry tools (Visio, Lucidchart, ER/Studio) | > [!TIP] > **KTU Examiner Tip**: For university exams, **Chen's notation is preferred** because it is the syllabus standard. However, if you draw Crow's Foot, label cardinality clearly to avoid ambiguity and loss of marks. # 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 The Five-Step Methodology for Schema Design The KTU 2024 lab manual mandates a **systematic five-step approach**. Following this sequence guarantees full marks in the design experiment. ### Step 1: Requirement Analysis (Read the Problem Carefully) - Read the problem description **twice**. - **Highlight nouns** → these are candidate **entities**. - **Highlight verbs** → these are candidate **relationships**. - **Highlight adjectives/descriptors** → these are candidate **attributes**. - Identify **business rules** (e.g., "each course is taught by exactly one professor"). ### Step 2: Identify Entities and Attributes - Filter out nouns that are actually attributes of another entity. - Example: In "the student has a name", *name* is an attribute of *Student*, not a separate entity. - **Classify attributes**: - **Simple / Atomic** — cannot be subdivided (e.g., age, roll_no) - **Composite** — can be subdivided (e.g., address → street, city, pincode) - **Multivalued** — multiple values (e.g., phone_numbers of a person) - **Derived** — computable from others (e.g., age from DOB) - **Key attribute** — uniquely identifies (e.g., roll_no) ### Step 3: Identify Relationships and Cardinality - For each pair of related entities, determine the **cardinality ratio**: - **1:1 (One-to-One)** — Each A relates to exactly one B and vice versa. Example: A person has one passport; a passport belongs to one person. - **1:N (One-to-Many)** — One A relates to many B, but each B relates to only one A. Example: One department has many professors. - **M:N (Many-to-Many)** — Many A relate to many B. Example: Students enroll in many courses; courses have many students. - Determine **participation constraint**: - **Total (mandatory)** — every entity instance must participate. Shown by a **double line** in Chen's notation. - **Partial (optional)** — some entities may not participate. Shown by a **single line**. ### Step 4: Draw the ER Diagram - Use rectangles for entities, ellipses for attributes, diamonds for relationships. - Underline primary key attributes. - Use double ellipses for multivalued, dashed ellipses for derived. - Draw double rectangles for weak entities, double diamonds for identifying relationships. ### Step 5: Convert ER to Relational Schema (Mapping) - This is the **most heavily tested** step in KTU lab exams. Apply the mapping rules below. ## 2.2 KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet: ER-to-Relational Mapping Rules > [!IMPORTANT] > These **7 mapping rules** are the *core algorithmic content* of KTU Module Experiment 2. Memorize them in this exact order. | Rule # | ER Construct | Mapping Action | Resulting Schema | |--------|--------------|----------------|------------------| | **R1** | Strong Entity Set E with primary key PK | Create a relation R(E) with PK as primary key | `R(PK, attr1, attr2, ...)` | | **R2** | Weak Entity Set W with owner E and partial key `pk` | Create relation W with composite key `(E.PK, W.pk)` | `W(E_PK, pk, attrs...)` | | **R3** | 1:1 Relationship R between E1 and E2 | Merge into either E1 or E2 by adding the other's PK as FK | `E1(PK1, ..., E2_PK)` | | **R4** | 1:N Relationship R between E1 (1-side) and E2 (N-side) | Add E1.PK as foreign key in E2 | `E2(PK2, ..., E1_PK)` | | **R5** | M:N Relationship R between E1 and E2 | Create a **new separate relation** with composite PK | `R(E1_PK, E2_PK, attrs...)` | | **R6** | Multivalued Attribute A of Entity E | Create a **new separate relation** with composite key `(E.PK, A)` | `E_A(E_PK, A, ...)` | | **R7** | n-ary Relationship (n > 2) | Create a new relation with PKs of all participating entities | `R(E1_PK, E2_PK, ..., En_PK)` | > [!WARNING] > **Critical Pitfall**: For 1:1 and 1:N, **NEVER** create a separate table. Only M:N and multivalued attributes require new tables. KTU examiners routinely deduct **2 marks** for this mistake. ## 2.3 Cardinality Notation Quick Reference $$ \text{Cardinality Ratio} \in \{ 1:1,\ 1:N,\ M:N \} $$ $$ \text{Participation Constraint} \in \{ \text{Total (double line)},\ \text{Partial (single line)} \} $$ > [!NOTE] > In **Crow's Foot notation**, the symbols are: > - `|` → **Exactly One** (mandatory participation, 1-side) > - `O\|` or `O` → **Zero or One** (optional 1-side) > - `<` (crow's foot) → **Many** (N-side or M-side) > - `O<` → **Zero or Many** (optional M-side) > > These map directly to SQL `JOIN` semantics when the schema is implemented. ## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility - **Banking Systems**: ER modeling is used to design accounts, customers, transactions, and loans before any SQL DDL is written. - **E-Commerce Platforms**: Entities like Customer, Order, Product, Cart, Payment, and Shipment are modeled first to ensure no data redundancy. - **Hospital Information Systems (HIS)**: Patient, Doctor, Ward, Prescription, and Appointment are ER-modeled to enforce referential integrity. - **University Management**: Student, Course, Faculty, Department, Enrollment, Exam — exactly the KTU lab problem domain. # 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix ## 3.1 Worked-Out Sample Problem (University Course Registration System) > [!NOTE] > **Problem Statement (KTU Model Question)**: > *"Design an ER diagram for a University database with the following description:* > *The University has several departments. Each department has a unique Dept_ID, name, and is headed by a professor (HOD). Every professor has a Prof_ID, name, salary, and belongs to exactly one department. Students have a Roll_No, name, and DOB. A student can enroll in many courses, and each course can have many students. Each course has a Course_ID, name, credits, and is taught by exactly one professor. A course belongs to exactly one department. Students must enroll in at least one course (total participation)."* ### Step 1: Identify Entities (Nouns) Extracting nouns: **University, Department, Professor, Student, Course**. - `University` → context, not an entity (treated as the entire scope). - `Department` → **Entity** (unique Dept_ID). - `Professor` → **Entity** (unique Prof_ID). - `Student` → **Entity** (unique Roll_No). - `Course` → **Entity** (unique Course_ID). **Analytical Matrix of Entities and Attributes:** | Entity | Primary Key | Other Attributes | Notes | |--------|-------------|------------------|-------| | **Department** | `Dept_ID` | `name`, `HOD_Prof_ID` (FK) | HOD is a professor, not a string | | **Professor** | `Prof_ID` | `name`, `salary` | Belongs to one department (1:N from Dept → Prof) | | **Student** | `Roll_No` | `name`, `DOB` | Enrolls in many courses | | **Course** | `Course_ID` | `name`, `credits` | Taught by one professor, belongs to one department | ### Step 2: Identify Relationships (Verbs) Extracting verbs and their cardinalities: | Relationship | Entity1 | Cardinality | Entity2 | Reasoning | |--------------|---------|-------------|---------|-----------| | `heads` | Department | **1:1** | Professor | A department has exactly one HOD; a prof heads at most one dept | | `works_in` | Department | **1:N** | Professor | One dept has many profs; each prof in one dept | | `enrolls_in` | Student | **M:N** | Course | A student takes many courses; a course has many students | | `teaches` | Professor | **1:N** | Course | One prof teaches many courses; each course taught by one prof | | `offers` | Department | **1:N** | Course | One dept offers many courses; each course in one dept | ### Step 3: Identify Participation Constraints | Relationship | Side | Participation | Reason | |--------------|------|---------------|--------| | `enrolls_in` | Student side | **Total** | "Students must enroll in at least one course" (explicit) | | `enrolls_in` | Course side | **Partial** | A new course may have no students yet | | `teaches` | Course side | **Total** | Every course is taught by exactly one professor | | `works_in` | Professor side | **Total** | Every professor belongs to a department | ### Step 4: Apply the 7 Mapping Rules (ER → Relational Schema) This is the **derivation step** — each rule is applied mechanically. **Rule R1 — Strong Entity Mapping:** $$ \text{Department}(\underline{\text{Dept\_ID}},\ \text{name}) $$ $$ \text{Professor}(\underline{\text{Prof\_ID}},\ \text{name},\ \text{salary}) $$ $$ \text{Student}(\underline{\text{Roll\_No}},\ \text{name},\ \text{DOB}) $$ $$ \text{Course}(\underline{\text{Course\_ID}},\ \text{name},\ \text{credits}) $$ **Rule R4 — 1:N Relationship (works_in, teaches, offers):** Add the "1-side" primary key as a foreign key on the "N-side" table. $$ \text{Professor}(\underline{\text{Prof\_ID}},\ \text{name},\ \text{salary},\ \text{Dept\_ID}^{\text{FK}}) $$ $$ \text{Course}(\underline{\text{Course\_ID}},\ \text{name},\ \text{credits},\ \text{Dept\_ID}^{\text{FK}},\ \text{Prof\_ID}^{\text{FK}}) $$ **Rule R3 — 1:1 Relationship (heads):** Add the HOD's `Prof_ID` as a foreign key in `Department`. $$ \text{Department}(\underline{\text{Dept\_ID}},\ \text{name},\ \text{HOD\_Prof\_ID}^{\text{FK}}) $$ **Rule R5 — M:N Relationship (enrolls_in):** Create a **new separate table** with composite primary key. $$ \text{Enrollment}(\underline{\text{Roll\_No}^{\text{FK}}},\ \underline{\text{Course\_ID}^{\text{FK}}},\ \text{enroll\_date},\ \text{grade}) $$ ### Step 5: Final Optimized Relational Schema $$ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &\textbf{Department}(\underline{\text{Dept\_ID}},\ \text{name},\ \text{HOD\_Prof\_ID}^{\text{FK}}) \\ &\textbf{Professor}(\underline{\text{Prof\_ID}},\ \text{name},\ \text{salary},\ \text{Dept\_ID}^{\text{FK}}) \\ &\textbf{Student}(\underline{\text{Roll\_No}},\ \text{name},\ \text{DOB}) \\ &\textbf{Course}(\underline{\text{Course\_ID}},\ \text{name},\ \text{credits},\ \text{Dept\_ID}^{\text{FK}},\ \text{Prof\_ID}^{\text{FK}}) \\ &\textbf{Enrollment}(\underline{\text{Roll\_No}^{\text{FK}}},\ \underline{\text{Course\_ID}^{\text{FK}}},\ \text{enroll\_date},\ \text{grade}) \end{aligned} } $$ **Foreign Key Constraint Summary (Analytical Matrix):** | Child Table | Foreign Key | References | Rule Applied | |-------------|-------------|------------|--------------| | Professor | `Dept_ID` | Department(Dept_ID) | R4 (1:N) | | Course | `Dept_ID` | Department(Dept_ID) | R4 (1:N) | | Course | `Prof_ID` | Professor(Prof_ID) | R4 (1:N) | | Department | `HOD_Prof_ID` | Professor(Prof_ID) | R3 (1:1) | | Enrollment | `Roll_No` | Student(Roll_No) | R5 (M:N part 1) | | Enrollment | `Course_ID` | Course(Course_ID) | R5 (M:N part 2) | ### Step 6: SQL DDL Implementation (Optional KTU Lab Extension) ```sql CREATE TABLE Department ( Dept_ID VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, HOD_Prof_ID VARCHAR(10), FOREIGN KEY (HOD_Prof_ID) REFERENCES Professor(Prof_ID) ); CREATE TABLE Professor ( Prof_ID VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, salary DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (salary > 0), Dept_ID VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID) ); CREATE TABLE Student ( Roll_No VARCHAR(15) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, DOB DATE NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE Course ( Course_ID VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, credits INT CHECK (credits > 0 AND credits <= 6), Dept_ID VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL, Prof_ID VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID), FOREIGN KEY (Prof_ID) REFERENCES Professor(Prof_ID) ); CREATE TABLE Enrollment ( Roll_No VARCHAR(15), Course_ID VARCHAR(10), enroll_date DATE NOT NULL, grade CHAR(2), PRIMARY KEY (Roll_No, Course_ID), FOREIGN KEY (Roll_No) REFERENCES Student(Roll_No), FOREIGN KEY (Course_ID) REFERENCES Course(Course_ID) ); ``` ## 3.2 Verification: The Mapping is Lossless The 7-rule algorithm is **provably lossless** — no information from the ER diagram is lost during conversion. This can be formally verified by checking: 1. Every entity has a relation. 2. Every attribute is placed in exactly one relation. 3. Every relationship is represented either as an FK or a separate table. 4. No null foreign key is forced in a 1:1 total participation scenario. # 4. Structural Diagrams & Schematics ## 4.1 ER Diagram (Chen's Notation — Mermaid Representation) > [!IMPORTANT] > The following Mermaid `erDiagram` block represents the **complete ER diagram** for the University problem. This is the diagram students must draw in the KTU lab record. Every line below should be transcribed into the lab record with proper rectangles, ellipses, and diamonds if Chen's notation is required by the examiner. ```mermaid erDiagram DEPARTMENT ||--o{ PROFESSOR : "works_in (1:N)" DEPARTMENT ||--o{ COURSE : "offers (1:N)" DEPARTMENT ||--|| PROFESSOR : "heads (1:1, HOD)" PROFESSOR ||--o{ COURSE : "teaches (1:N)" STUDENT }o--o{ COURSE : "enrolls_in (M:N, Student side TOTAL)" DEPARTMENT { string Dept_ID PK string name string HOD_Prof_ID FK } PROFESSOR { string Prof_ID PK string name decimal salary string Dept_ID FK } STUDENT { string Roll_No PK string name date DOB } COURSE { string Course_ID PK string name int credits string Dept_ID FK string Prof_ID FK } ENROLLMENT { string Roll_No PK,FK string Course_ID PK,FK date enroll_date string grade } STUDENT ||--o{ ENROLLMENT : "has" COURSE ||--o{ ENROLLMENT : "has" ``` ## 4.2 Block-Level Functional Architecture Flow (ER-to-Schema Pipeline) This diagram shows the **five-stage transformation pipeline** from raw problem statement to executable SQL DDL. It is the exact sequence students should follow during the KTU lab viva and record submission. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Step 1: Read Problem Statement] --> B[Step 2: Extract Nouns and Verbs] B --> C[Step 3: Classify into Entities, Attributes, Relationships] C --> D[Step 4: Determine Cardinality and Participation] D --> E[Step 5: Draw ER Diagram in Chen Notation] E --> F[Step 6: Apply the 7 Mapping Rules] F --> G[Step 7: Generate Relational Schema with Keys] G --> H[Step 8: Write SQL CREATE TABLE Statements] H --> I[Step 9: Add Constraints PK FK NOT NULL CHECK] I --> J[Step 10: Verify Lossless Join Property] A1[NLP Tokenization] -.-> A B1[Highlight Nouns Entities] -.-> B B2[Highlight Verbs Relationships] -.-> B B3[Highlight Adjectives Attributes] -.-> B C1[Filter Out Anomalies] -.-> C D1[1:1, 1:N, M:N Ratios] -.-> D D2[Total vs Partial] -.-> D F1[R1 Strong Entity] -.-> F F2[R3 1:1 Relationship] -.-> F F3[R4 1:N Relationship] -.-> F F4[R5 M:N New Table] -.-> F F5[R6 Multivalued New Table] -.-> F style A fill:#FFE4B5 style E fill:#98FB98 style G fill:#87CEEB style J fill:#FFB6C1 ``` ## 4.3 Cardinality Decision Tree (Analytical Aid) Use this decision tree to determine the correct cardinality for each relationship in your ER diagram during the KTU exam. ```mermaid flowchart TD Q1{Is one instance of A
related to at most one B?} Q1 -- Yes --> Q2{Is one instance of B
related to at most one A?} Q1 -- No --> M1[Many-to-Many M:N] M1 --> M1note[CREATE new table R with
composite PK A.PK, B.PK] Q2 -- Yes --> OneOne[1:1 Relationship] Q2 -- No --> Q3{Is one B related
to many A?} Q3 -- Yes --> OneMany[1:N Relationship
A is 1-side, B is N-side] Q3 -- No --> Q4{Re-evaluate problem statement} Q4 --> Q1 OneOne --> O1[Merge: Add A.PK as FK in B
OR B.PK as FK in A] OneMany --> O2[Add A.PK as FK in B table
Total participation implies NOT NULL] style OneOne fill:#FFD700 style OneMany fill:#FFD700 style M1 fill:#90EE90 style M1note fill:#FFB6C1 style O1 fill:#ADD8E6 style O2 fill:#ADD8E6 ``` # 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap ## 5.1 Part A Questions (3 Marks Each) --- ### **Q1. [KTU University Exam - May 2024]** **Define the following with one example each:** **(a) Entity and Entity Set** **(b) Total Participation** **Model Answer:** **(a)** An **Entity** is a real-world object with independent existence that can be uniquely identified. Example: A specific student named "Rahul" with roll number `S001` is an entity. An **Entity Set** is a collection of similar entities. Example: The set of all students currently enrolled in a college is a *Student* entity set. **(b)** **Total Participation** means every entity in the entity set must participate in at least one instance of the relationship. It is represented by a **double line** connecting the entity to the relationship diamond in Chen's notation. Example: In a "Department-Employs-Professor" relationship, every Professor must belong to some department (total participation of Professor in *employs*). --- ### **Q2. [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]** **Differentiate between strong entity and weak entity with suitable examples.** **Model Answer:** | Feature | Strong Entity | Weak Entity | |---------|---------------|-------------| | **Existence** | Has independent existence | Depends on a strong (owner) entity | | **Identifier** | Has a primary key of its own | Cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes alone | | **Notation** | Single rectangle | Double rectangle | | **Relationship** | Not dependent | Connected to owner via a **double-diamond identifying relationship** | | **Example** | `Student(Roll_No, name, DOB)` — Roll_No is sufficient PK | `Dependent(Dep_Name, age, Emp_ID)` — needs `Emp_ID` from `Employee` plus `Dep_Name` to form PK | --- ## 5.2 Part B Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice) --- ### **Question A (14 Marks) — [KTU University Exam - May 2024 Model]** > **Design an ER diagram for the following Library Management System and convert it into a relational schema:** > > *"A library has multiple branches, each with a unique branch_id and location. Each branch holds many books. A book is identified by ISBN and has a title, price, and a single category. A book can be written by many authors, and an author can write many books. A book may have multiple copies, and each copy has a copy_id and a shelf location. Members of the library have a member_id, name, and phone (a member can have multiple phone numbers). A member can borrow many book copies, and a copy can be borrowed by many members over time. Each borrowing records the issue_date and return_date."* #### **Part (a) — Draw the complete ER diagram with all entities, attributes, relationships, cardinalities, and participation constraints. (7 Marks)** **Step 1 — Identify Entities:** - `Branch` (branch_id, location) - `Book` (ISBN, title, price, category) - `Author` (author_id, name) - `Book_Copy` (copy_id, ISBN_FK, branch_id_FK, shelf_location) - `Member` (member_id, name) - `Borrow` (issue_date, return_date, member_id_FK, copy_id_FK) **Step 2 — Identify Relationships:** | Relationship | Between | Cardinality | Participation | |--------------|---------|-------------|---------------| | `has` | Branch — Book_Copy | 1:N | Book_Copy side **Total** | | `written_by` | Book — Author | M:N | Both **Partial** | | `borrows` | Member — Book_Copy | M:N (with attributes) | Both **Partial** | **Step 3 — Special Attributes:** - `phone` in Member is a **multivalued attribute** (double ellipse). - `Book_Copy` is a **weak entity** (double rectangle) with partial key `copy_id`, depending on Book and Branch. **Step 4 — ER Diagram in Mermaid:** ```mermaid erDiagram BRANCH ||--o{ BOOK_COPY : "holds (1:N)" BOOK ||--o{ BOOK_COPY : "has_copies (1:N, identifying)" BOOK }o--o{ AUTHOR : "written_by (M:N)" MEMBER }o--o{ BOOK_COPY : "borrows (M:N with Borrow attrs)" MEMBER ||--o{ MEMBER_PHONE : "has (multivalued)" BRANCH { string branch_id PK string location } BOOK { string ISBN PK string title decimal price string category } AUTHOR { string author_id PK string name } BOOK_COPY { string copy_id PK string ISBN PK,FK string branch_id PK,FK string shelf_location } MEMBER { string member_id PK string name } MEMBER_PHONE { string member_id PK,FK string phone PK } BORROW { string member_id PK,FK string copy_id PK,FK string ISBN PK,FK string branch_id PK,FK date issue_date date return_date } ``` #### **Part (b) — Convert the above ER diagram into a fully normalized relational schema with primary keys, foreign keys, and constraint specification. (7 Marks)** **Applying the 7 Mapping Rules:** ```sql -- Rule R1: Strong Entities CREATE TABLE Branch ( branch_id VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, location VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE Book ( ISBN VARCHAR(13) PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL, price DECIMAL(8,2) CHECK (price > 0), category VARCHAR(50) ); CREATE TABLE Author ( author_id VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE Member ( member_id VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL ); -- Rule R2: Weak Entity (Book_Copy depends on Book and Branch) CREATE TABLE Book_Copy ( copy_id VARCHAR(10), ISBN VARCHAR(13), branch_id VARCHAR(10), shelf_location VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (ISBN, branch_id, copy_id), FOREIGN KEY (ISBN) REFERENCES Book(ISBN), FOREIGN KEY (branch_id) REFERENCES Branch(branch_id) ); -- Rule R5: M:N Relationship (written_by) CREATE TABLE Book_Author ( ISBN VARCHAR(13), author_id VARCHAR(10), PRIMARY KEY (ISBN, author_id), FOREIGN KEY (ISBN) REFERENCES Book(ISBN), FOREIGN KEY (author_id) REFERENCES Author(author_id) ); -- Rule R6: Multivalued Attribute (phone) CREATE TABLE Member_Phone ( member_id VARCHAR(10), phone VARCHAR(15), PRIMARY KEY (member_id, phone), FOREIGN KEY (member_id) REFERENCES Member(member_id) ); -- Rule R5: M:N Relationship with attributes (borrows) CREATE TABLE Borrow ( member_id VARCHAR(10), copy_id VARCHAR(10), ISBN VARCHAR(13), branch_id VARCHAR(10), issue_date DATE NOT NULL, return_date DATE, PRIMARY KEY (member_id, copy_id, ISBN, branch_id, issue_date), FOREIGN KEY (member_id) REFERENCES Member(member_id), FOREIGN KEY (copy_id, ISBN, branch_id) REFERENCES Book_Copy(copy_id, ISBN, branch_id) ); ``` **Final Optimized Relational Schema:** $$ \boxed{ \begin{aligned} &\textbf{Branch}(\underline{\text{branch\_id}},\ \text{location}) \\ &\textbf{Book}(\underline{\text{ISBN}},\ \text{title},\ \text{price},\ \text{category}) \\ &\textbf{Author}(\underline{\text{author\_id}},\ \text{name}) \\ &\textbf{Book\_Copy}(\underline{\text{ISBN}^{\text{FK}}},\ \underline{\text{branch\_id}^{\text{FK}}},\ \underline{\text{copy\_id}},\ \text{shelf\_location}) \\ &\textbf{Member}(\underline{\text{member\_id}},\ \text{name}) \\ &\textbf{Member\_Phone}(\underline{\text{member\_id}^{\text{FK}}},\ \underline{\text{phone}}) \\ &\textbf{Book\_Author}(\underline{\text{ISBN}^{\text{FK}}},\ \underline{\text{author\_id}^{\text{FK}}}) \\ &\textbf{Borrow}(\underline{\text{member\_id}^{\text{FK}}},\ \underline{\text{copy\_id}^{\text{FK}}},\ \underline{\text{ISBN}^{\text{FK}}},\ \underline{\text{branch\_id}^{\text{FK}}},\ \underline{\text{issue\_date}},\ \text{return\_date}) \end{aligned} } $$ --- ### **Question B (14 Marks) — [KTU University Exam - Dec 2023 Model]** > **Design an ER diagram and relational schema for the following Hospital Management System:** > > *"A hospital has many departments, each with a Dept_ID, name, and location. Each department has multiple doctors, identified by Doc_ID, name, specialization, and salary. A doctor treats many patients, and a patient can be treated by multiple doctors. A patient has a Pat_ID, name, age, and may have multiple phone numbers. Patients are admitted to rooms. A room has a room_no, type (general/ICU/private), and a daily charge. A patient may be admitted multiple times (each admission has an admission_id, admit_date, and discharge_date). Each admission is to exactly one room, but a room can host many admissions over time."* #### **Part (a) — Identify all entities, attributes (including multivalued and derived), relationships, cardinalities, and participation. Draw the ER diagram. (7 Marks)** **Entities & Attributes:** | Entity | Primary Key | Other Attributes | |--------|-------------|------------------| | Department | `Dept_ID` | `name`, `location` | | Doctor | `Doc_ID` | `name`, `specialization`, `salary` | | Patient | `Pat_ID` | `name`, `age` (derived from DOB), `DOB`, `phone` (multivalued) | | Room | `room_no` | `type`, `daily_charge` | | Admission | `admission_id` | `admit_date`, `discharge_date` | **Relationships & Cardinalities:** | Relationship | Cardinality | Participation | Notes | |--------------|-------------|---------------|-------| | Department — Doctor | 1:N | Doctor side **Total** | Each doctor belongs to one dept | | Doctor — Patient (treats) | M:N | Both **Partial** | Many-to-many treatment relationship | | Patient — Room (admitted_via) | M:N (through Admission) | Patient side **Total** (during admission) | Need association entity Admission | | Admission — Room | 1:N (one admission → one room; one room → many admissions) | Admission side **Total** | Each admission is to exactly one room | **Derived attribute:** `age` is derived from `DOB` (shown with dashed ellipse). **Multivalued attribute:** `phone` of Patient (shown with double ellipse). **ER Diagram (Mermaid):** ```mermaid erDiagram DEPARTMENT ||--o{ DOCTOR : "employs (1:N)" DOCTOR }o--o{ PATIENT : "treats (M:N)" PATIENT ||--o{ ADMISSION : "has (1:N, identifying)" ROOM ||--o{ ADMISSION : "hosts (1:N)" PATIENT ||--o{ PATIENT_PHONE : "has (multivalued)" DEPARTMENT { string Dept_ID PK string name string location } DOCTOR { string Doc_ID PK string name string specialization decimal salary string Dept_ID FK } PATIENT { string Pat_ID PK string name date DOB int age } PATIENT_PHONE { string Pat_ID PK,FK string phone PK } ROOM { string room_no PK string type decimal daily_charge } ADMISSION { string admission_id PK string Pat_ID PK,FK string room_no PK,FK date admit_date date discharge_date } ``` #### **Part (b) — Convert the ER diagram to a normalized relational schema and write the corresponding SQL DDL. (7 Marks)** ```sql -- R1: Strong Entities CREATE TABLE Department ( Dept_ID VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, location VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE Doctor ( Doc_ID VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, specialization VARCHAR(50), salary DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (salary > 0), Dept_ID VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY (Dept_ID) REFERENCES Department(Dept_ID) ); CREATE TABLE Patient ( Pat_ID VARCHAR(15) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, DOB DATE NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE Room ( room_no VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, type VARCHAR(20) CHECK (type IN ('General', 'ICU', 'Private')), daily_charge DECIMAL(8,2) CHECK (daily_charge >= 0) ); -- R5: M:N Doctor-Patient (treats) CREATE TABLE Treatment ( Doc_ID VARCHAR(10), Pat_ID VARCHAR(15), treatment_date DATE, diagnosis TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (Doc_ID, Pat_ID, treatment_date), FOREIGN KEY (Doc_ID) REFERENCES Doctor(Doc_ID), FOREIGN KEY (Pat_ID) REFERENCES Patient(Pat_ID) ); -- R6: Multivalued phone CREATE TABLE Patient_Phone ( Pat_ID VARCHAR(15), phone VARCHAR(15), PRIMARY KEY (Pat_ID, phone), FOREIGN KEY (Pat_ID) REFERENCES Patient(Pat_ID) ); -- R1 + R4: Admission (associative entity linking Patient and Room) CREATE TABLE Admission ( admission_id VARCHAR(15) PRIMARY KEY, Pat_ID VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL, room_no VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL, admit_date DATE NOT NULL, discharge_date DATE, FOREIGN KEY (Pat_ID) REFERENCES Patient(Pat_ID), FOREIGN KEY (room_no) REFERENCES Room(room_no) ); ``` > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls** > 1. **M:N Trap**: Students often treat `Doctor–Patient` as 1:N because "one doctor treats many patients" — but forget that "one patient can be treated by many doctors". This makes it **M:N** and **REQUIRES a separate `Treatment` table**. (Penalty: −2 marks) > 2. **Multivalued Attribute Neglect**: Forgetting to create `Patient_Phone` for the `phone` attribute. In SQL, this violates **1NF**. (Penalty: −1 mark) > 3. **Weak Entity Confusion**: Treating `Admission` as a strong entity. It is a strong entity here (it has its own PK `admission_id`), but `Book_Copy` in the previous question was a weak entity. Read the problem carefully! (Penalty: −1 mark) > 4. **Missing Cardinality Labels**: Drawing relationships without `1:1`, `1:N`, `M:N` labels. (Penalty: −1 mark) > 5. **FK Notation**: Writing `FOREIGN KEY` but forgetting to mark it as FK in the schema box. Always annotate with `FK` superscript. (Penalty: −1 mark) > 6. **Derived Attribute**: Storing `age` in the table. Derived attributes must be **computed at query time**, not stored. (Penalty: −1 mark) --- ## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember > [!TIP] > **High-Density Rapid Revision Checklist — KTU Module Experiment 2** ### ER Modeling Essentials - ☐ **Entity = Noun**, **Attribute = Adjective**, **Relationship = Verb** - ☐ Primary key must be **underlined** in the ER diagram - ☐ **Multivalued** = double ellipse, **Derived** = dashed ellipse, **Composite** = ellipse with sub-ellipses - ☐ **Weak entity** = double rectangle, **Identifying relationship** = double diamond - ☐ **Cardinality** must be explicitly written: 1:1, 1:N, M:N - ☐ **Participation** must be shown: single line (partial) or double line (total) ### Mapping Rules (The 7 Commandments) - ☐ **R1** — Every strong entity → one table - ☐ **R2** — Weak entity → table with composite PK `(owner_PK, partial_key)` - ☐ **R3** — 1:1 relationship → merge (add FK to either side) - ☐ **R4** — 1:N relationship → add 1-side PK as FK on N-side - ☐ **R5** — M:N relationship → **new separate table** with composite PK - ☐ **R6** — Multivalued attribute → **new separate table** with `(entity_PK, attribute)` - ☐ **R7** — n-ary relationship (n ≥ 3) → new table with all participating PKs ### Schema Writing Best Practices - ☐ Always specify **PRIMARY KEY** and **FOREIGN KEY** constraints - ☐ Use **NOT NULL** for mandatory attributes (e.g., name, primary keys) - ☐ Use **CHECK** constraints for domain validation (e.g., `salary > 0`, `credits BETWEEN 1 AND 6`) - ☐ Choose appropriate **data types**: `VARCHAR`, `INT`, `DECIMAL`, `DATE`, `CHAR` - ☐ Composite primary keys are written as `PRIMARY KEY (col1, col2)` - ☐ Foreign key references must match the referenced table's column(s) ### KTU Exam-Specific Reminders - ☐ Draw ER diagram **before** writing the schema — **always** - ☐ Use **Chen's notation** by default (rectangles + diamonds + ellipses) - ☐ Label every relationship with a verb and cardinality - ☐ If using Crow's Foot, label with `|, O|, <, O<` symbols - ☐ For SQL DDL questions, include all constraints in `CREATE TABLE` statements - ☐ Do **not** include sample data (`INSERT` statements) unless asked - ☐ Verify normalization — the schema should be in **3NF** minimum - ☐ Common exam duration: 3 hours, full experiment should be solvable in 45 minutes ### Quick Memory Trick > 🎯 **"1:1 Merge, 1:N FK, M:N New"** — Repeat this 10 times before the exam. ### Bonus Conceptual Check - ☐ Can you identify a **recursive relationship**? (e.g., Employee supervises Employee) - ☐ Can you identify a **ternary relationship**? (e.g., Doctor prescribes Drug to Patient — all 3 entities) - ☐ Can you convert a **generalization/specialization** hierarchy to a schema? (Use "ISA" relationship)

# Section 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology)

**Data Manipulation Language (DML)** is a subset of the Structured Query Language (SQL) used in Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS) to **retrieve, insert, modify, and delete data** stored within the existing schema objects (tables, views) of a database. Unlike Data Definition Language (DDL), which alters the *structure* of database objects, DML operates strictly on the *data content* (rows/tuples) of those objects.

The four canonical DML operations are collectively referred to as **CRUD**:
- **C**reate → `INSERT`
- **R**ead → `SELECT`
- **U**pdate → `UPDATE`
- **D**elete → `DELETE`

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU 2024 Syllabus Highlight (PCCSL408 – Module 2):**
> The experiment mandates hands-on practice of `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `ALTER` (table modification to support new data), `DELETE`, and conditional `SELECT` queries. While `ALTER` is technically a DDL command, it is grouped under "data manipulation practices" in the KTU lab manual because it is required to *accommodate* new data during experimentation.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Core Definitional Distinction (Frequently Tested):**
> - **DML (Data Manipulation Language):** Manipulates *data* inside tables. Commands: `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`.
> - **DDL (Data Definition Language):** Manipulates *structure* of tables. Commands: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`.
> - **DCL (Data Control Language):** Manages *permissions*. Commands: `GRANT`, `REVOKE`.
> - **TCL (Transaction Control Language):** Manages *transactions*. Commands: `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`, `SAVEPOINT`.

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Office Filing Cabinet" Model

Imagine a **library's card catalog system**:

| Database Concept | Real-World Analogy |
|---|---|
| **Table** | A single filing drawer labelled "Student Records" |
| **Row/Tuple** | One individual student's complete file card |
| **Column/Attribute** | A specific field on the card (Name, Roll No, Marks) |
| **INSERT** | Filing a brand new student's card into the drawer |
| **SELECT** | Searching and reading existing cards without moving them |
| **UPDATE** | Erasing an old phone number on a card and writing the new one |
| **DELETE** | Removing a card permanently from the drawer |
| **ALTER** | Adding a new column "Email" to every card in the drawer (a structural upgrade) |
| **WHERE clause** | The search filter — e.g., "only show cards where Marks > 80" |

> [!TIP]
> **Intuitive Takeaway:** DML commands never change the *shape* of the drawer (number of compartments), only the *cards inside it*. The exception is `ALTER`, which KTU groups here because in lab practice you often need to expand the drawer to store new kinds of information.

## 1.3 Key Terminology Inventory (Board-Exam Vocabulary)

- **Tuple / Record / Row:** A single horizontal entry in a table.
- **Attribute / Field / Column:** A vertical named entity in a table schema.
- **Predicate (WHERE clause condition):** A Boolean expression that evaluates to TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN for each row.
- **ACID Properties:** Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — governing DML execution under transactions.
- **Cardinality:** The number of rows in a relation (modified by INSERT/DELETE).
- **Arity / Degree:** The number of columns in a relation (modified by ALTER).
- **Commit:** Permanent saving of DML changes to the database.
- **Rollback:** Undoing uncommitted DML changes.

---

# Section 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Syntax Sheet

## 2.1 The DML Command Architecture

SQL DML operations follow a strict logical pipeline. Every `UPDATE` and `DELETE` statement **must** include a `WHERE` clause in practice, otherwise the operation affects *every row* in the table — a classic board-exam pitfall.

### 2.1.1 Operational Logic Flow of a DML Statement

1. **Parse** → SQL engine checks syntax and semantic validity.
2. **Optimize** → Query Optimizer generates the most efficient execution plan.
3. **Execute** → Rows are located, locked, modified, and written to the **buffer cache** (not yet on disk).
4. **Commit / Rollback** → The transaction is finalized or aborted.

## 2.2 The INSERT Command — Theory of Operation

`INSERT` appends new tuples to a relation. There are two syntactic variants:

**Variant A — Column-list specified (RECOMMENDED, board-safe):**
```sql
INSERT INTO table_name (col1, col2, col3)
VALUES (val1, val2, val3);
```

**Variant B — Positional (all columns, in declaration order):**
```sql
INSERT INTO table_name VALUES (val1, val2, val3);
```

**Variant C — Multi-row bulk insert (efficient, KTU favorite):**
```sql
INSERT INTO table_name (col1, col2) VALUES
  (val_a, val_b),
  (val_c, val_d),
  (val_e, val_f);
```

**Variant D — Insert from a SELECT (subquery-based):**
```sql
INSERT INTO target_table (col1, col2)
SELECT src_col1, src_col2
FROM source_table
WHERE condition;
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Constraint Enforcement Rule:** If a column has a `NOT NULL` constraint and no `DEFAULT` value, omitting it from the column list will cause the INSERT to fail with an integrity constraint violation. This is a common KTU viva question.

## 2.3 The UPDATE Command — Theory of Operation

`UPDATE` modifies values of existing rows. Syntax skeleton:
```sql
UPDATE table_name
SET col1 = new_value1 [, col2 = new_value2, ...]
[WHERE condition];
```

**Evaluation Order:**
1. The DBMS scans the table (or uses an index).
2. The `WHERE` clause is evaluated **row by row** to identify candidate tuples.
3. Matching rows are locked (in transactional systems).
4. New values replace old values in the in-memory row.
5. The change is logged in the **transaction log** for redo/undo purposes.

> [!WARNING]
> **The "Forgot the WHERE" Catastrophe:**
> Running `UPDATE Student SET Marks = 100;` (no WHERE) will assign 100 to *every* student. In Oracle/MySQL, the command executes unless a `SAFE_UPDATES` mode is active. KTU examiners specifically test this trap.

## 2.4 The DELETE Command — Theory of Operation

```sql
DELETE FROM table_name
[WHERE condition];
```

**Critical Distinction:**

| Command | Effect | Rollback Possible? | Resets Identity? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DELETE FROM table WHERE ...` | Removes selected rows | Yes (within uncommitted txn) | No |
| `DELETE FROM table;` (no WHERE) | Removes all rows | Yes | No |
| `TRUNCATE TABLE table;` | Removes all rows | **No** (implicit commit) | **Yes** |
| `DROP TABLE table;` | Removes table + data + structure | No | Yes |

> [!NOTE]
> **Board Tip:** The difference between `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE`, and `DROP` is one of the most frequently asked 3-mark questions in KTU ESE papers.

## 2.5 The SELECT Command — Conditional Querying

The `SELECT` statement is the "Read" half of CRUD. Basic syntax:
```sql
SELECT [DISTINCT] col1, col2, aggregate(col3)
FROM table_name
[WHERE row_condition]
[GROUP BY col]
[HAVING group_condition]
[ORDER BY col [ASC | DESC]];
```

**Key Clauses — Evaluation Order (interview + viva favorite):**
1. `FROM` → Identify source tables.
2. `WHERE` → Filter individual rows.
3. `GROUP BY` → Form groups.
4. `HAVING` → Filter groups.
5. `SELECT` → Choose columns / compute aggregates.
6. `DISTINCT` → Remove duplicates.
7. `ORDER BY` → Sort final result.

> **Mnemonic:** ***"From Wisconsin, George Has Sorted Data"*** — **F**rom, **W**here, **G**roup by, **H**aving, **S**elect, **D**istinct, **O**rder by.

## 2.6 The ALTER Command — Structural Modification (Lab Context)

Although classified as DDL, KTU's Module 2 includes it because lab experiments often require schema evolution to support richer data:

```sql
-- Add a new column
ALTER TABLE Student ADD Email VARCHAR(50);

-- Modify data type / size
ALTER TABLE Student MODIFY Phone VARCHAR(15);

-- Drop a column
ALTER TABLE Student DROP COLUMN Email;

-- Rename a column (MySQL 8+ / Oracle 10g+)
ALTER TABLE Student RENAME COLUMN Phone TO Mobile;
```

## 2.7 KTU High-Yield Syntax Cheat Sheet (Board-Exam Quick Reference)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The following table summarizes the precise syntax skeletons that must be reproduced verbatim in KTU lab records and theory exams. **Memorize the brackets [ ] as "optional" and the pipes { } as "choose one".**

| Command | Syntax Skeleton | Affects | Reversible? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `INSERT` | `INSERT INTO T [(c1,c2)] VALUES (v1,v2) [, (v3,v4)]` | Row count ↑ | Yes (rollback) |
| `UPDATE` | `UPDATE T SET c1=v1 [WHERE cond]` | Column values of rows | Yes (rollback) |
| `DELETE` | `DELETE FROM T [WHERE cond]` | Row count ↓ | Yes (rollback) |
| `SELECT` | `SELECT cols FROM T [WHERE cond] [ORDER BY c]` | None (read-only) | N/A |
| `ALTER` | `ALTER TABLE T ADD / MODIFY / DROP COLUMN c` | Schema structure | Yes (rollback in some DBs) |

## 2.8 Real-World Engineering Utility

DML commands form the operational backbone of virtually every enterprise system:

- **Banking Systems:** `UPDATE Account SET Balance = Balance - 5000 WHERE AccNo = 101;` — atomic money transfers.
- **E-Commerce:** `INSERT INTO Orders (...) VALUES (...);` — recording customer purchases.
- **Healthcare (Aarogya Setu / HMIS):** `SELECT * FROM Patients WHERE District = 'Ernakulam' AND Age > 60;` — disease surveillance queries.
- **University ERP (KTU's own):** `UPDATE StudentResult SET GPA = 8.7 WHERE RollNo = 'TVE21CS001';`

# Section 3: Step-by-Step Analytical Walkthroughs & Query Construction

> [!NOTE]
> Since this is a **DBMS Lab** topic, "derivations" are reframed as **exhaustive query construction walkthroughs** showing every logical and syntactic transition.

## 3.1 Reference Schema (Used in All Walkthroughs)

To make the experiment reproducible, assume the following KTU-standard lab schema:

```sql
CREATE TABLE Student (
    RollNo   VARCHAR(10)  PRIMARY KEY,
    Name     VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    Dept     VARCHAR(20),
    Age      INT,
    Marks    INT,
    Grade    CHAR(2)
);
```

## 3.2 Walkthrough 1 — Constructing an INSERT Statement

**Problem:** Insert a record: `('S001', 'Anand Krishna', 'CSE', 20, 85, 'A')`.

**Step-by-step reasoning:**

**Step 1** — Identify the target table and required columns.
The statement must operate on the `Student` table. Since we have data for every column, we can either:
- Use the short form (positional, all 6 values in order), OR
- Use the long form (explicit column list — **safer for exams**).

**Step 2** — Match value count to column count.
Six columns → six values. Mismatch raises a column-count error in MySQL/Oracle.

**Step 3** — Wrap string values in single quotes; numerics need no quotes.

**Step 4** — Final SQL:
```sql
INSERT INTO Student (RollNo, Name, Dept, Age, Marks, Grade)
VALUES ('S001', 'Anand Krishna', 'CSE', 20, 85, 'A');
```

**Step 5** — Verify outcome: `SELECT * FROM Student;` should display 1 row.

**Variant — Bulk insert (KTU bonus credit):**
```sql
INSERT INTO Student (RollNo, Name, Dept, Age, Marks, Grade) VALUES
('S002', 'Divya R',   'CSE', 21, 92, 'A'),
('S003', 'Rahul M',   'ECE', 22, 78, 'B'),
('S004', 'Sneha P',   'CSE', 20, 65, 'C'),
('S005', 'Vivek N',   'MECH',23, 55, 'D'),
('S006', 'Anjali T',  'CSE', 21, 88, 'A');
```

## 3.3 Walkthrough 2 — Constructing a Conditional UPDATE

**Problem:** Increase the `Marks` of all `CSE` students by 5 (grade boost).

**Step 1** — Identify target table → `Student`.
**Step 2** — Identify the modification → `Marks` column, new value = `Marks + 5` (use existing column in expression).
**Step 3** — Identify filter condition → `Dept = 'CSE'`.
**Step 4** — Construct the SQL:
```sql
UPDATE Student
SET Marks = Marks + 5
WHERE Dept = 'CSE';
```

**Step 5 — Logical verification (pre/post state):**

$$
\text{Rows Affected} = \vert \text{\{rows where Dept = 'CSE'\}} \vert
$$

| RollNo | Name | Dept | Marks (Before) | Marks (After) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S001 | Anand Krishna | CSE | 85 | **90** |
| S002 | Divya R | CSE | 92 | **97** |
| S003 | Rahul M | ECE | 78 | 78 (unchanged) |
| S004 | Sneha P | CSE | 65 | **70** |
| S005 | Vivek N | MECH | 55 | 55 (unchanged) |
| S006 | Anjali T | CSE | 88 | **93** |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Cardinality Preservation Property:** An `UPDATE` statement **never changes the number of rows** in a table. Only `INSERT` (adds) and `DELETE` (removes) alter cardinality. This is a board-exam short-answer favorite.

## 3.4 Walkthrough 3 — Constructing a DELETE Statement

**Problem:** Remove all students who scored below the passing threshold (Marks < 40).

**Step 1** — Target: `Student` table.
**Step 2** — Filter: `Marks < 40`.
**Step 3** — Construct:
```sql
DELETE FROM Student
WHERE Marks < 40;
```

**Step 4** — Cardinality change:
$$
\text{Cardinality}_{\text{after}} = \text{Cardinality}_{\text{before}} - \vert \text{\{rows where Marks} < 40\} \vert
$$

> [!TIP]
> **Recovery Pattern (Examiners love this):** Before any `DELETE` in a real lab, execute `SELECT * FROM Student WHERE Marks < 40;` first to *preview* the victims. This is a professional habit KTU evaluators appreciate.

## 3.5 Walkthrough 4 — Constructing a Conditional SELECT

**Problem:** Display the RollNo, Name, and Marks of CSE students whose marks are between 70 and 90, sorted in descending order of marks.

**Step 1** — Required output columns → `RollNo, Name, Marks`.
**Step 2** — Source table → `Student`.
**Step 3** — Row filter → `Dept = 'CSE' AND Marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90`.
**Step 4** — Sort order → `Marks DESC`.
**Step 5** — Compose:
```sql
SELECT RollNo, Name, Marks
FROM Student
WHERE Dept = 'CSE' AND Marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90
ORDER BY Marks DESC;
```

**Step 6 — Logical operator precedence in WHERE clause (critical for board exams):**

In SQL, Boolean operators are evaluated in this priority:

$$
\text{NOT} \;>\ \; \text{AND} \;>\ \; \text{OR}
$$

**Rule of thumb:**
$$
\text{Evaluate NOT first, then AND, finally OR.}
$$

**Example trap:**
```sql
-- This query WITHOUT parentheses:
SELECT * FROM Student WHERE Dept = 'CSE' OR Dept = 'ECE' AND Marks > 80;
-- Is interpreted as:
--   Dept = 'CSE'  OR  (Dept = 'ECE' AND Marks > 80)
-- NOT as:
--   (Dept = 'CSE' OR Dept = 'ECE') AND Marks > 80
```

> [!WARNING]
> **Always use parentheses** to make Boolean logic explicit. The KTU valuation key explicitly deducts marks for ambiguous predicates.

## 3.6 Walkthrough 5 — Multi-row UPDATE with Subquery (Advanced)

**Problem:** Promote all students with Marks > 90 to Grade 'A+'.

```sql
UPDATE Student
SET Grade = 'A+'
WHERE Marks > 90;
```

**Verification approach:** Always pair DML with a SELECT in the lab record:
```sql
-- PRE-CHECK
SELECT RollNo, Name, Marks, Grade FROM Student WHERE Marks > 90;
-- EXECUTE UPDATE
UPDATE Student SET Grade = 'A+' WHERE Marks > 90;
-- POST-CHECK
SELECT RollNo, Name, Marks, Grade FROM Student WHERE Marks > 90;
```

## 3.7 Walkthrough 6 — ALTER + INSERT Combined Workflow

A typical KTU lab cycle uses `ALTER` to expand the schema, then `INSERT` to populate the new field.

```sql
-- Step 1: Add a new column to accommodate email
ALTER TABLE Student ADD Email VARCHAR(50);

-- Step 2: Populate the new column for an existing student
UPDATE Student SET Email = 'anand@kerala.ac.in' WHERE RollNo = 'S001';

-- Step 3: Insert a brand new student WITH the email value
INSERT INTO Student (RollNo, Name, Dept, Age, Marks, Grade, Email)
VALUES ('S007', 'Lakshmi B', 'CSE', 20, 91, 'A+', 'lakshmi@kerala.ac.in');
```

## 3.8 Analytical Matrix — Operator Reference Table

| Operator | SQL Symbol | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equality | `=` | `WHERE Dept = 'CSE'` | Exact match |
| Inequality | `<>` or `!=` | `WHERE Dept <> 'CSE'` | Not equal |
| Range | `BETWEEN x AND y` | `WHERE Marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90` | Inclusive range |
| Set membership | `IN (a,b,c)` | `WHERE Dept IN ('CSE','ECE')` | Value in list |
| Pattern | `LIKE 'pattern'` | `WHERE Name LIKE 'A%'` | String match (% = any, _ = one) |
| Null test | `IS NULL / IS NOT NULL` | `WHERE Email IS NULL` | Missing value |
| Logical AND | `AND` | `A AND B` | Both must be TRUE |
| Logical OR | `OR` | `A OR B` | At least one TRUE |
| Logical NOT | `NOT` | `NOT (Marks > 80)` | Inversion |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **NULL vs Zero vs Empty String:**
> - `NULL` is the *absence of a value* — it is **not equal to 0**, **not equal to ''** (empty string), and **not equal to another NULL**.
> - Use `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL` — never `= NULL` (this is a KTU classic error).

---

<!-- SECTION_3_END -->

# Section 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics

## 4.1 DML Command Classification Tree

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[SQL SUBSYSTEM] --> B[DML]
    A --> C[DDL]
    A --> D[DCL]
    A --> E[TCL]
    B --> F[INSERT]
    B --> G[SELECT]
    B --> H[UPDATE]
    B --> I[DELETE]
    F --> F1[Single Row]
    F --> F2[Multi Row Bulk]
    F --> F3[From Subquery SELECT]
    G --> G1[All Columns Asterisk]
    G --> G2[Specific Columns]
    G --> G3[With WHERE Filter]
    G --> G4[With ORDER BY Sort]
    G --> G5[With GROUP BY Aggregation]
    H --> H1[Single Column]
    H --> H2[Multiple Columns]
    H --> H3[With Subquery]
    I --> I1[Conditional WHERE]
    I --> I2[All Rows no WHERE]
    C --> J[ALTER]
    J --> J1[ADD COLUMN]
    J --> J2[MODIFY COLUMN]
    J --> J3[DROP COLUMN]
    J --> J4[RENAME COLUMN]
```

## 4.2 DML Statement Execution Pipeline (Block Diagram)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[User Issues SQL Statement] --> B[Parser]
    B --> C{Syntax Valid?}
    C -->|No| D[Return Error]
    C -->|Yes| E[Query Optimizer]
    E --> F[Execution Engine]
```

# Section 5: KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU 2024 Assessment Pattern Reference:**
> - **Part A (3 marks):** Short answer / definition / small SQL snippet.
> - **Part B (14 marks):** Full lab-cycle question with internal choice; typically asks to (a) write 5–6 SQL statements [7 marks] + (b) explain output / write more queries / discuss error scenarios [7 marks].

---

## Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2024]
**Differentiate between DDL and DML commands in SQL. Give two examples of each.**

**Model Answer (Verbatim expected phrasing):**

> **DDL (Data Definition Language)** is used to define, alter, or drop the *structure* of database objects such as tables, schemas, and indexes. DDL statements are **auto-committed** in most RDBMS, meaning changes cannot be rolled back. Examples: `CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP TABLE`.
>
> **DML (Data Manipulation Language)** is used to *manipulate the data* stored inside the existing schema objects. DML statements operate on rows/records and are **transactional** — they can be rolled back before commit. Examples: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `SELECT`.
>
> **Key Distinction:** DDL changes the *schema*; DML changes the *data* within an unchanged schema.

### Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023]
**What is the difference between `DELETE`, `TRUNCATE`, and `DROP` commands in SQL?**

**Model Answer:**

| Aspect | DELETE | TRUNCATE | DROP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Type | DML | DDL | DDL |
| Removes | Selected rows (or all) | All rows | Entire table + data + structure |
| WHERE clause | Allowed | Not allowed | Not applicable |
| Rollback | Yes (within uncommitted txn) | No (implicit commit) | No (implicit commit) |
| Resets auto-increment | No | Yes | Yes (table gone) |
| Speed | Slowest (row-by-row, logs each) | Faster (deallocates pages) | Fastest |
| Syntax | `DELETE FROM T WHERE ...` | `TRUNCATE TABLE T` | `DROP TABLE T` |

---

## Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each — Internal Choice)

### QUESTION A — [KTU Model ESE Question — Module 2 Pattern]

**(a) [7 Marks]** Consider the following table schema for a college database:
```
Employee(EmpID INT PK, Name VARCHAR(40), Department VARCHAR(20), Salary INT, JoiningDate DATE)
```
Write SQL DML statements for the following:
1. Insert three employee records using a single INSERT statement.
2. Increase the salary of all employees in the 'CSE' department by 10%.
3. Delete the record of the employee whose EmpID is 105.
4. Display the Name and Salary of employees earning more than 50,000, sorted by Salary descending.
5. Display the count of employees in each department.

**(b) [7 Marks]** What will be the output of query (4) and (5) if the table currently contains the data shown below? Explain each query step-by-step.

| EmpID | Name | Department | Salary | JoiningDate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 101 | Anand | CSE | 55000 | 2021-06-12 |
| 102 | Divya | ECE | 48000 | 2020-03-05 |
| 103 | Rahul | CSE | 72000 | 2019-07-22 |
| 104 | Sneha | MECH | 39000 | 2022-01-15 |
| 105 | Vivek | CSE | 30000 | 2023-08-01 |

#### Model Solution for (a):

**1. Insert three employee records using a single INSERT statement:**
```sql
INSERT INTO Employee (EmpID, Name, Department, Salary, JoiningDate) VALUES
(101, 'Anand',  'CSE',  55000, '2021-06-12'),
(102, 'Divya',  'ECE',  48000, '2020-03-05'),
(103, 'Rahul',  'CSE',  72000, '2019-07-22');
```

**2. Increase salary of all CSE employees by 10%:**
```sql
UPDATE Employee
SET Salary = Salary * 1.10
WHERE Department = 'CSE';
```
*Logic: `Salary * 1.10` = `Salary + (Salary * 0.10)` = original salary plus 10% increment.*

**3. Delete the record where EmpID = 105:**
```sql
DELETE FROM Employee
WHERE EmpID = 105;
```

**4. Display Name and Salary of employees with Salary > 50000, sorted by Salary DESC:**
```sql
SELECT Name, Salary
FROM Employee
WHERE Salary > 50000
ORDER BY Salary DESC;
```

**5. Display the count of employees in each department:**
```sql
SELECT Department, COUNT(*) AS EmployeeCount
FROM Employee
GROUP BY Department;
```

#### Model Solution for (b):

**Query 4 Output:**

Step 1: `FROM Employee` → load all 5 rows.
Step 2: `WHERE Salary > 50000` → keep rows with Salary 55000 (Anand), 72000 (Rahul); reject 48000, 39000, 30000.
Step 3: `SELECT Name, Salary` → output these two columns.
Step 4: `ORDER BY Salary DESC` → sort by salary in descending order.

| Name | Salary |
|---|---|
| Rahul | 72000 |
| Anand | 55000 |

**Query 5 Output:**

Step 1: `FROM Employee` → all 5 rows.
Step 2: `GROUP BY Department` → partition rows into {CSE: Anand, Rahul, Vivek} and {ECE: Divya} and {MECH: Sneha}.
Step 3: `COUNT(*)` per group → 3, 1, 1.
Step 4: `SELECT Department, COUNT(*)` → output the group identifier and count.

| Department | EmployeeCount |
|---|---|
| CSE | 3 |
| ECE | 1 |
| MECH | 1 |

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Where Students Lose Marks:**
> 1. **Forgetting commas in multi-row INSERT** — each tuple must be comma-separated.
> 2. **Using `=` instead of `IS` for NULL** — e.g., `WHERE Email = NULL` is *always* FALSE; use `IS NULL`.
> 3. **Missing WHERE clause in UPDATE/DELETE** — instant 2-mark penalty even if the rest is correct.
> 4. **Quoting strings** — `'CSE'` (with quotes), not `CSE` (treated as a column name).
> 5. **Using `HAVING` where `WHERE` is required** — `HAVING` filters *groups*, `WHERE` filters *rows*.

---

### QUESTION B — [Alternative Choice — Same Marks Pattern]

**(a) [7 Marks]** Consider the table:
```
Product(PID INT PK, PName VARCHAR(30), Category VARCHAR(20), Price INT, Stock INT)
```
Write SQL DML statements to:
1. Add a new column `Supplier` of type VARCHAR(40) to the Product table.
2. Insert four products with appropriate values for all columns.
3. Update the Price of all products in the 'Electronics' category by reducing it by 15%.
4. Delete all products whose Stock is 0.
5. Display the PName and Price of the top 3 most expensive products.

**(b) [7 Marks]** Explain the difference between the `WHERE` and `HAVING` clauses with a suitable example. Also, write a query to display, for each category, the average price of products that have an average price greater than 1000.

#### Model Solution for (a):

**1. Add Supplier column:**
```sql
ALTER TABLE Product ADD Supplier VARCHAR(40);
```

**2. Insert four products:**
```sql
INSERT INTO Product (PID, PName, Category, Price, Stock, Supplier) VALUES
(201, 'Laptop A',    'Electronics', 65000, 12, 'Dell India'),
(202, 'Mouse B',     'Electronics',   450, 80, 'Logitech'),
(203, 'Notebook C',  'Stationery',     60, 500, 'Classmate'),
(204, 'Pen Drive D', 'Electronics',   550,  0, 'Sandisk');
```

**3. Reduce Electronics price by 15%:**
```sql
UPDATE Product
SET Price = Price * 0.85
WHERE Category = 'Electronics';
```
*Logic: `Price * 0.85` = 85% of original = 15% reduction.*

**4. Delete products with Stock = 0:**
```sql
DELETE FROM Product
WHERE Stock = 0;
```

**5. Top 3 most expensive products:**
```sql
SELECT PName, Price
FROM Product
ORDER BY Price DESC
LIMIT 3;
```
*(In Oracle, use `FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY`; in SQL Server, use `SELECT TOP 3 ...`.)*

#### Model Solution for (b):

**WHERE vs HAVING — Theoretical Distinction:**

| Aspect | WHERE | HAVING |
|---|---|---|
| Filters | Individual rows | Groups (post-GROUP BY) |
| Used with | Any DML/SELECT | Only with GROUP BY / aggregates |
| Aggregate functions allowed? | **No** | **Yes** |
| Execution order | Before GROUP BY | After GROUP BY |
| Example | `WHERE Price > 500` | `HAVING AVG(Price) > 1000` |

**Example query — Average price per category > 1000:**
```sql
SELECT Category, AVG(Price) AS AvgPrice
FROM Product
GROUP BY Category
HAVING AVG(Price) > 1000;
```

**Step-by-step evaluation:**

Step 1: `FROM Product` — load all rows.
Step 2: `GROUP BY Category` — partition into groups {Electronics, Stationery}.
Step 3: `AVG(Price)` per group — Electronics = (65000+450+550)/3 = 22000; Stationery = 60.
Step 4: `HAVING AVG(Price) > 1000` — keep Electronics (22000 > 1000); discard Stationery (60 < 1000).

**Output:**

| Category | AvgPrice |
|---|---|
| Electronics | 22000 |

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Pitfall Callout — `ALTER TABLE` Mistakes:**
> 1. **Wrong DBMS syntax:** MySQL uses `ADD`, Oracle uses `ADD` (same), but some older PostgreSQL requires `ADD COLUMN`. KTU lab uses MySQL/Oracle primarily — write portable syntax.
> 2. **Forgetting `COLUMN` keyword:** `ALTER TABLE T DROP Email` may fail in strict mode. Always say `DROP COLUMN Email`.
> 3. **Trying to ALTER a non-existent table** — common when the experiment is run in the wrong schema.

## Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!TIP]
> **High-Density Revision Checklist — Pin This Before the Exam:**

- **DML = Data Manipulation Language** = works on data inside tables: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `SELECT`.
- **DDL = Data Definition Language** = works on table structure: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`.
- **CRUD mapping:** Create→`INSERT`, Read→`SELECT`, Update→`UPDATE`, Delete→`DELETE`.
- **Always include a `WHERE` clause** in `UPDATE` and `DELETE` to avoid mass modification (KTU favorite trap).
- **String literals use single quotes** `'CSE'`; numeric values do not need quotes.
- **NULL is the absence of value** — test with `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`, never `= NULL`.
- **Boolean precedence in WHERE:** `NOT > AND > OR` — use parentheses for clarity.
- **`LIKE` wildcards:** `%` = any sequence of characters; `_` = exactly one character.
- **`BETWEEN` is inclusive** of both endpoints.
- **`DISTINCT`** removes duplicate rows in SELECT output.
- **`ORDER BY`** default is ASC; specify `DESC` for descending.
- **Clause evaluation order in SELECT:** FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY.
- **DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP:** row-level / table-data / full-table including structure.
- **Bulk INSERT** is faster than multiple single-row INSERTs.
- **Multi-table UPDATE / DELETE** can use subqueries with `IN` or `EXISTS` (advanced KTU viva point).
- **COMMIT makes DML changes permanent**; `ROLLBACK` undoes uncommitted changes.
- **Lab record must always pair every DML with a verification SELECT** to earn full marks.
- **Use uppercase for SQL keywords** in the lab record — improves readability and KTU valuation goodwill.

## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Set Operators in SQL

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Scheme):** *Set operators in SQL are specialized keywords (UNION, UNION ALL, INTERSECT, EXCEPT) that combine the result sets of two or more SELECT statements into a single output by performing mathematical set theory operations (union, intersection, difference) on the retrieved tuples.*

**Conceptual Analogy / Intuition:**
Imagine two circles in a Venn diagram, each containing a list of names. The `UNION` operator is like throwing both circles into a big box and removing duplicate names (keeping only unique ones). `UNION ALL` keeps every name, even duplicates. `INTERSECT` keeps only those names that appear in **both** circles. `EXCEPT` (or `MINUS`) keeps names that are in the **first** circle but **not** in the second. Just like a Venn diagram, the "circles" here are the result sets of two SELECT queries.

> [!NOTE]
> **Core Compatibility Rule:** For set operators to work, both SELECT statements **must** have the same number of columns, and the corresponding columns must have compatible (or implicitly convertible) data types.

### 1.2 Nested Queries (Subqueries)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Scheme):** *A nested query, or subquery, is a SELECT statement embedded within another SQL statement (such as SELECT, FROM, WHERE, or HAVING clause). The inner query executes first and returns a value (or a set of values) that the outer query uses to perform its final retrieval.*

**Conceptual Analogy / Intuition:**
Think of it as asking a two-step question. First, you ask your friend, *"What is the salary of the highest-paid employee?"* (this is the **inner/subquery**). Once you get the answer (say, ₹90,000), you then ask yourself, *"Show me everyone who earns more than ₹90,000"* (this is the **outer query**). The outer query depends on the result of the inner query to function. This is the essence of nesting.

### 1.3 Join Queries

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Scheme):** *A join is an operation that combines rows from two or more related tables based on a common column (typically a Primary Key to Foreign Key relationship) using a predicate, producing a single composite result set that spans multiple tables.*

**Conceptual Analogy / Intuition:**
Imagine two spreadsheets. The first has Employee IDs and Names. The second has Employee IDs and Salaries. A join is like using a *glue column* (the matching Employee ID) to stitch the spreadsheets side by side, so you end up with one big sheet containing ID, Name, **and** Salary together. The "glue" is the join condition (`ON` clause).

### 1.4 Reference Schema Used in KTU Lab

> - **PROJECT** (Pno PK, Pname, PLocation, DeptNo FK)

## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Set Operators — Deep Breakdown

**Set Theory Foundations in SQL:**

| Operator | Mathematical Notation | Behaviour | Duplicate Handling |
|----------|----------------------|-----------|--------------------|
| `UNION` | $A \cup B$ | Combines all rows from both queries | Removes duplicates automatically |
| `UNION ALL` | $A \cup B$ (with multiplicity) | Combines all rows | Keeps duplicates |
| `INTERSECT` | $A \cap B$ | Returns only common rows | Removes duplicates |
| `EXCEPT` (or `MINUS` in Oracle) | $A - B$ | Returns rows in Query1 not in Query2 | Removes duplicates |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Why "removes duplicates" matters:** Set operators treat result sets as *true mathematical sets*. By default, SQL assumes set semantics (no duplicates), so the engine incurs the cost of an implicit `DISTINCT` sort. If you need speed and don't care about duplicates, use `UNION ALL` — it skips the dedup step and is significantly faster.

**The "Why" behind the Column Matching Rule:**
SQL performs set operations column-by-column positionally (left to right), not by column name. So `SELECT Ename FROM EMP` cannot be `UNION`-ed with `SELECT Salary FROM EMP` — the first column is a string, the second is a number. The number of columns and the data type *family* of each corresponding position must match.

**KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet:**

| Construct | General Syntax Template | Pre-Requisite Rule | Typical Use Case |
|-----------|------------------------|--------------------|------------------|
| Set Operator | $Q_1 \ \text{OP} \ Q_2$ | $\mid \text{cols}(Q_1) \mid = \mid \text{cols}(Q_2) \mid$ | Combining two result sets |
| `UNION` | `SELECT ... UNION SELECT ...` | Same column count + compatible types | Employees in dept 10 OR 20 |
| `UNION ALL` | `SELECT ... UNION ALL SELECT ...` | Same as UNION (faster) | Audit logs, append-only history |
| `INTERSECT` | `SELECT ... INTERSECT SELECT ...` | Same as UNION | Employees in BOTH projects A and B |
| `EXCEPT` | `SELECT ... EXCEPT SELECT ...` | Same as UNION | Employees in project A but NOT B |
| `IN` (subquery) | `WHERE col IN (SELECT col FROM ...)` | Subquery returns list | Multi-row membership test |
| Scalar Subquery | `SELECT (SELECT ... FROM ... LIMIT 1) FROM ...` | Subquery returns one value | Computed column |
| `INNER JOIN` | `FROM A JOIN B ON A.x = B.y` | Match condition required | Default cross-table query |
| `LEFT JOIN` | `FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON ...` | Preserves left rows | Find unmatched (orphans) |
| `SELF JOIN` | `FROM A T1 JOIN A T2 ON ...` | Same table, two aliases | Manager-Employee hierarchy |

### 2.2 Nested Queries — Deep Breakdown

**Types of Subqueries (High-Yield for KTU):**

1. **Single-Row Subquery** — returns exactly **one row** and **one column**. Use with `=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`, `<>`.
   *Example:* Find employees earning the maximum salary.

2. **Multi-Row Subquery** — returns **multiple rows**, but one column. Use with `IN`, `ANY`, `ALL`.
   *Example:* Find employees working in departments located in 'Kochi'.

3. **Multi-Column Subquery** — returns **multiple columns**. Use with `IN` and a tuple comparison.
   *Example:* Find employees having the same (Job, DeptNo) as someone else.

4. **Correlated Subquery** — the inner query references a column from the **outer query**. It executes **once per row** of the outer query.
   *Example:* Find employees earning more than the average salary of *their own department*.

5. **Subquery in FROM clause (Derived Table)** — the inner query acts as a virtual table.
   *Example:* `SELECT * FROM (SELECT DeptNo, AVG(Salary) AS avg_sal FROM EMP GROUP BY DeptNo) AS t WHERE avg_sal > 50000;`

> [!NOTE]
> **Why correlated subqueries are slow:** Because the inner query re-executes for *every* row of the outer table, complexity can become $O(n^2)$. For large tables, KTU examiners often expect you to prefer a `JOIN` with a `GROUP BY` instead.

### 2.3 Join Queries — Deep Breakdown

**Logical Equivalence Cheat Sheet (KTU loves these!):**

| SQL Construct | Equivalent Form | When to Use |
|---------------|-----------------|-------------|
| `WHERE A.x = B.x` (in multi-table `FROM`) | `INNER JOIN` | Old-style implicit join |
| `LEFT JOIN + WHERE B.x IS NULL` | `NOT EXISTS` / `EXCEPT` | Anti-join: rows in A not matched in B |
| `IN (SELECT ...)` | Semi-join | Membership test |
| `EXISTS (SELECT ...)` | Semi-join with early exit | Existence check (often faster) |
| Scalar subquery in `SELECT` | `LEFT JOIN` with grouping | Computed columns across tables |

**Real-World Engineering Utility:**
- **Set Operators** → Used in ETL pipelines, merging partitioned data, audit reporting.
- **Nested Queries** → Used in dynamic dashboards (filter based on aggregated sub-results).
- **Joins** → The backbone of any OLTP system — assembling a single screen (e.g., an order with customer, product, and shipping details) from normalized tables.

## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Worked Example — Set Operators (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)

**Problem:** Find the names of employees who are in Department 10 **OR** Department 20.

**Logical derivation:**

$$
\text{Result} = \{e.\text{Ename} \mid e.\text{DeptNo} = 10\} \cup \{e.\text{Ename} \mid e.\text{DeptNo} = 20\}
$$

**Step 1:** Identify the two sub-queries (the two circles of the Venn diagram).
- Circle A: Employees in Dept 10.
- Circle B: Employees in Dept 20.

**Step 2:** Verify compatibility — both queries select 1 column (`Ename`), same data type (`VARCHAR`).

**Step 3:** Apply the `UNION` operator.

```sql
SELECT Ename FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE DeptNo = 10
UNION
SELECT Ename FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE DeptNo = 20;
```

**Analytical Matrix — Behaviour of the three operators on identical input:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Input A} &= \{ \text{Anu, Bala, Anu} \} \\
\text{Input B} &= \{ \text{Bala, Chitra} \} \\
\text{A UNION B} &= \{ \text{Anu, Bala, Chitra} \} \quad \text{(Anu appears once)} \\
\text{A UNION ALL B} &= \{ \text{Anu, Bala, Anu, Bala, Chitra} \} \quad \text{(5 rows)} \\
\text{A INTERSECT B} &= \{ \text{Bala} \} \\
\text{A EXCEPT B} &= \{ \text{Anu} \}
\end{aligned}
$$

> [!NOTE]
> Observe that `EXCEPT` (also called `MINUS` in Oracle) is **not symmetric**: `A EXCEPT B` ≠ `B EXCEPT A`. Always check the order of operands.

---

### 3.2 Worked Example — Nested Subquery

**Problem:** Find the names of employees who earn more than the average salary of the entire company.

**Logical derivation:**

$$
\text{Result} = \{e.\text{Ename} \mid e.\text{Salary} > \bar{S}\}, \quad \text{where} \quad \bar{S} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i.\text{Salary}
$$

**Step 1 (Inner query — compute the scalar):** The average salary is a single number.

```sql
SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE;   -- returns one row, one column, e.g., 55000
```

**Step 2 (Outer query — apply the filter):** Treat the scalar as a constant.

```sql
SELECT Ename FROM EMPLOYEE
WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM EMPLOYEE);
```

**Step 3 (Execution flow):**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Phase 1 (Inner):} \quad & \bar{S} \leftarrow 55000 \\
\text{Phase 2 (Outer):} \quad & \text{Filter rows where Salary} > 55000 \\
& \Rightarrow \text{returns } \{ \text{Bala, Chitra, David} \}
\end{aligned}
$$

---

### 3.3 Worked Example — Correlated Subquery

**Problem:** Find employees who earn more than the average salary of **their own** department.

**Logical derivation:**

$$
\text{Result} = \{e.\text{Ename} \mid e.\text{Salary} > \text{AVG}(\text{Salary in } e.\text{DeptNo})\}
$$

**Step 1:** Notice the inner query references `e.DeptNo` from the outer query — this is a *correlation*.

```sql
SELECT Ename, Salary, DeptNo
FROM EMPLOYEE AS e1
WHERE Salary > (
    SELECT AVG(Salary)
    FROM EMPLOYEE AS e2
    WHERE e2.DeptNo = e1.DeptNo   -- <-- correlation link
);
```

**Step 2 (Execution flow, per row):**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Outer row: } e_1 = (\text{Anu, 60000, 10}) & \Rightarrow \text{inner computes AVG where DeptNo=10} \rightarrow 55000 \\
& \Rightarrow 60000 > 55000 \rightarrow \text{include Anu} \\
\text{Outer row: } e_1 = (\text{Eve, 40000, 10}) & \Rightarrow 40000 > 55000 \rightarrow \text{exclude Eve}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3 (Equivalent JOIN rewrite — faster for large tables):**

```sql
SELECT e1.Ename, e1.Salary
FROM EMPLOYEE e1
JOIN (
    SELECT DeptNo, AVG(Salary) AS avg_sal
    FROM EMPLOYEE
    GROUP BY DeptNo
) AS d ON e1.DeptNo = d.DeptNo
WHERE e1.Salary > d.avg_sal;
```

---

### 3.4 Worked Example — Joins (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL)

**Problem:** Display employee name and their department name for all employees.

**Step 1 — INNER JOIN (default, only matching rows):**

```sql
SELECT e.Ename, d.Dname
FROM EMPLOYEE e
INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON e.DeptNo = d.DeptNo;
```

**Step 2 — LEFT JOIN (all employees, even if no department match):**

```sql
SELECT e.Ename, d.Dname
FROM EMPLOYEE e
LEFT JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON e.DeptNo = d.DeptNo;
```

**Step 3 — RIGHT JOIN (all departments, even if no employee):**

```sql
SELECT e.Ename, d.Dname
FROM EMPLOYEE e
RIGHT JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON e.DeptNo = d.DeptNo;
```

**Step 4 — FULL OUTER JOIN (all employees AND all departments):**

```sql
SELECT e.Ename, d.Dname
FROM EMPLOYEE e
FULL OUTER JOIN DEPARTMENT d ON e.DeptNo = d.DeptNo;
```

**Set-Theoretic Venn Equivalence for Joins:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{INNER JOIN} &= A \cap B \\
\text{LEFT JOIN} &= A \cup (A \cap B) \\
\text{RIGHT JOIN} &= B \cup (A \cap B) \\
\text{FULL OUTER JOIN} &= A \cup B \\
\text{LEFT JOIN WHERE B.x IS NULL} &= A - B
\end{aligned}
$$

---

### 3.5 Analytical Matrix — Operator Selection Guide

| Requirement | Best Tool | Reason |
|-------------|-----------|--------|
| Combine two filter lists, dedup needed | `UNION` | Set semantics |
| Combine two filter lists, keep all rows | `UNION ALL` | Faster (no dedup) |
| Find rows common to two conditions | `INTERSECT` | Direct set intersection |
| Find rows in A but not in B | `EXCEPT` | Set difference |
| Filter based on a computed aggregate | Scalar subquery | Returns single value |
| Filter based on a dynamic list | `IN` subquery | Returns multi-row, single column |
| Show one-to-many relationship | `INNER JOIN` | Combines matching rows |
| Find orphans (unmatched rows) | `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL` | Preserves left, NULL on right |
